meta.theme: the sense of direct access to a character's mind explained by the deletion of the reporting verb rather than by the doubling of voices, with the same deletion removing the warrant that makes an unreliable report detectable, a prediction about neutral diction offered as a test, and the word illusion restricted to its optical sense

meta.reviewer_notes: The rival explanation is conceded in full and then shown to answer a different question, which keeps it live for the agreement and title questions. The hardest move is the fourth paragraph, where the same subtraction that creates the effect destroys the warrant, so the passage's most positive claim and its most uncomfortable one share a mechanism. The closing paragraph restricts the word illusion and refuses two conclusions a reader will have begun to draw.

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option that the sense of access survives where the idiom belongs to nobody in particular, which the fifth paragraph denies by predicting and reporting the opposite; the key instead runs the fourth paragraph forward, since a sentence that makes no claim offers nothing for a doubt to attach to. Q2's rival is the title about why some novelists persuade us, which names exactly the question the last paragraph says the account cannot answer. Q3's rival is the option that the device gives a reader knowledge other modes withhold, which inverts the mechanism: nothing is added to the characterisation, and the effect is produced by a deletion. Q4's rival is the option extending the account to every mode of representing thought, which cannot hold, since the explanation is the absence of a verb the other modes contain. Q5's exception is the claim that the device was developed to conceal the narrator's judgements, a purpose the passage never states and which contradicts the rival account it concedes, where the novelist remains present in the sentence. Q6's rival is the option about novelists praised for depth, which supports the account the passage rejects, that something has been added.

paragraphs.text: Ask a reader what happened in a novel and you get a summary. Ask what it was like, and with certain novels and not others you get a different kind of answer: not that the book told them what somebody thought, but that they were inside the thinking while it was going on. The effect is peculiar, it is reported consistently, and it belongs to a technique with an ugly name. Set the same moment down three ways. I shall have to answer it tonight, she thought. She thought that she would have to answer it that night. The letter would have to be answered tonight; there was no getting round it. Only the third produces the effect, and readers who cannot name the difference can feel it.

The explanation usually given is about the author. Because the third sentence carries the character's idiom inside the narrator's grammar, two voices occupy it at once, and a novelist can therefore remain present in a sentence he appears to have vacated, colouring a thought without interrupting it. That is true, and it is worth knowing, and it is an account of what the device does for the writer. It does not explain what the sentence does to the reader. A reader who feels close to a mind is not registering the author's continued presence. If anything the sensation is of the author's absence, which is the very thing the usual account was framed to deny.

The explanation of the sensation is grammatical, and it is negative. Both of the first two sentences contain a verb of reporting. A verb of reporting names an agent, and an agent implies a channel: somebody has taken the thought and passed it on, and a reader who is given a channel will place a distance along it, however short. The third sentence deletes that verb and keeps everything else, the character's words, her rhythm, her exasperation, all of it inside the narrator's tense and person. Nothing in the sentence names a transmitter. There is consequently nowhere for the reader to locate the mediation, and a thought with no visible carrier is experienced as arriving directly. The access is manufactured by a subtraction. Nothing whatever has been added to the characterisation.

The subtraction removes something else in the same stroke, and this is the part usually missed. A verb of reporting is also a warrant. When a narrator says that she thought something, the narrator has undertaken that she did, and the undertaking can be false, which is what makes an unreliable report detectable: there is a claim on the page to be disbelieved. The free indirect sentence makes no such claim and offers nobody to have got it wrong. So the mode that gives a reader the strongest sense of knowing a mind is exactly the mode in which the reader has least to go on, and unreliability inside it does not present itself as error. It is simply not visible.

An account of this kind earns its keep by predicting where the effect fails, and this one does. If the sensation depends on the idiom being unmistakably the character's, it ought to weaken wherever a sentence might have been produced by either party. That is what happens. Passages in which the diction is neutral, in which nothing is phrased as this person and not another would phrase it, are read as commentary however faithfully they keep the grammatical form, and what the reader senses is a narrator thinking about a character rather than a character thinking. The rival account predicts nothing of the kind, since two voices inhabit the neutral sentence exactly as they inhabit the vivid one.

Two limits should be entered here, and the first is a limit on the word illusion. It is meant as an optician means it, a reliable appearance with a known mechanism, and not as a trick played on anybody. No claim is made in such a sentence, so there is nothing in it that could be a lie, and a reader who feels close to a character has not been imposed upon. The second limit is the larger one. The account explains the sensation and not the achievement. Why one novelist's pages in this mode read like a mind and another's like a man doing an impression is a question about the ear, and nothing in the grammar answers it. What the grammar explains is why the good ones are able to work at all, which is a smaller thing and was worth establishing.

questions.target_mistake: keeping the passage's claim about the strength of the effect and dropping its claim about what the same deletion takes away
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the inference will follow from the missing warrant: with no claim on the page, a reader has nothing to disbelieve.
questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.A: Quoted thought is a less truthful way of representing a consciousness than the third form is
options.B: A reader who doubts what a character believes about herself has nothing in such a sentence to attach the doubt to
options.C: Novelists took up the technique in order to make unreliable narration possible in the first place
options.D: A passage whose idiom belongs to nobody in particular will still be experienced as direct access

explanation.expert_notice: The fourth paragraph turns on a single equivalence: a verb of reporting is also a warrant, and a warrant is an undertaking that can be false. Take the verb away and there is no undertaking, which the paragraph states plainly by saying the sentence makes no such claim and offers nobody to have got it wrong.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option runs that consequence down to the reader. Doubt needs something to fasten on, and what it fastens on in the other modes is a narrator's assertion that a character thought something. Where no assertion has been made, a reader's suspicion has no place in the sentence to sit, which is why the paragraph says unreliability here is not an error one detects but something simply not visible.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question rewards taking a stated mechanism one step towards its consequence for somebody. Where a passage says what a form does not contain, ask what could not be done without it.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage explains an effect by a deletion, ask what else the deleted thing was doing. Authors who notice a second function for it put the passage's hardest inference there.

distractors.why_wrong: No comparison of truthfulness is made anywhere. The passage compares what each form contains, a verb of reporting or none, and says the third makes no claim at all, which places it outside the scale on which truthfulness is measured.
distractors.seductive_element: The fourth paragraph is full of warrants, undertakings and falsity, which reads like a discussion of accuracy rather than of what a sentence commits anyone to.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage says nothing about anybody's intentions in adopting the device. It explains a grammatical consequence and notes that unreliability becomes invisible, which is an effect of the form rather than a purpose anyone is said to have had.
distractors.seductive_element: The paragraph moves from the device straight to unreliable narration, and a reader accustomed to explanations by purpose supplies the motive the passage leaves out.

distractors.why_wrong: The fifth paragraph predicts and then reports the reverse. Where the diction is neutral, the passage is read as commentary however faithfully it keeps the form, and what the reader senses is a narrator thinking about a character.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the third paragraph locates the effect in the missing verb, which invites a reader to conclude that the missing verb is sufficient on its own.

questions.target_mistake: titling the passage from the explanation it concedes, or from the question its final paragraph says the account cannot answer
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: a title has to name the effect and the deletion that produces it, since every paragraph after the second depends on both.
questions.stem: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?

options.A: The Two Voices in a Single Sentence
options.B: Why Some Novelists Persuade Us and Others Do Not
options.C: The Access That a Missing Verb Creates
options.D: The Deception at the Heart of the Novel

explanation.expert_notice: The passage names an effect in its first paragraph, refuses one explanation of it in the second, supplies another in the third, draws a consequence in the fourth, tests it in the fifth and bounds it in the sixth. The one thing present in every movement after the first is the deleted verb.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct title names the effect and its cause in the passage's own terms. Access is the word for what readers report, and the missing verb is what the explanation turns on, which is also what the consequence about warrants and the prediction about neutral diction both depend on. A title that drops either half loses four of the six paragraphs.
explanation.question_type_note: A title is the main idea under a word limit, so altitude decides it. Too low and it names a paragraph; drawn from the conceded account, it names the position the passage is correcting.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask what each candidate title would make the passage about, and then check whether the author wrote that passage. The conceded explanation and the acknowledged limit both make attractive titles for essays nobody here has written.

distractors.why_wrong: This names the usual explanation, which the second paragraph grants and then sets aside as an account of what the device does for the writer rather than of what it does to the reader. As a title it would announce the position the passage exists to supplement.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the familiar description of the technique, the passage states it sympathetically and calls it worth knowing, and nothing in the second paragraph declares it false.

distractors.why_wrong: The last paragraph names this as precisely the question the account cannot answer, calling it a question about the ear that nothing in the grammar addresses. A title cannot be built from the passage's own disclaimer.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it sounds like the interesting literary question and because the passage raises it explicitly, which makes it feel like the destination rather than the boundary.

distractors.why_wrong: The sixth paragraph forbids exactly this reading of the word illusion, saying it is meant as an optician means it, that no claim is made and nothing in the sentence could be a lie, and that the reader has not been imposed upon.
distractors.seductive_element: The fourth paragraph's account of invisible unreliability sounds like a charge, and a reader who has felt its force will read the closing correction as a softening rather than as a definition.

questions.target_mistake: attributing to the author the view he concedes, or the added-depth account his explanation is built to replace
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict agreement with a statement about an effect produced by removal rather than by addition.
questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which of the following statements?

options.A: The technique lets a reader know things about a character that the other two forms keep back
options.B: A device can produce its effect by leaving something out rather than by putting something in
options.C: The novel would be an honester form if every report of a thought were marked as a report
options.D: What the device is chiefly for is letting a novelist mock a character and pity her in one breath

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph states the author's position twice in consecutive sentences, once positively and once negatively: the access is manufactured by a subtraction, and nothing whatever has been added to the characterisation. The fourth paragraph then finds a second effect of the same subtraction.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that position stated as a general principle, which is the level at which agreement questions work. The whole explanation depends on the deleted verb and on nothing else being different, and the paragraph is careful to deny that any content has been supplied, which is why the same passage can produce a stronger sensation of knowing while giving the reader less to go on.
explanation.question_type_note: An agreement question lives on the line between what an author reports and what he holds. Sort each option into his claim, his concession, or the view he is replacing before choosing.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask which sentence of the passage each option would have to be built from. An option that can only be built from the paragraph where the author states somebody else's view is a distractor however plausible it sounds.

distractors.why_wrong: The effect is real and its cause has been reversed. The passage says nothing has been added to the characterisation, and the fourth paragraph goes further, making this the mode in which the reader has least to go on.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because feeling that you know a character better is exactly what readers report, and the option simply converts the feeling into the knowledge it feels like.

distractors.why_wrong: The final paragraph rules out the judgement this rests on, insisting that no claim is made in such a sentence, that nothing in it could be a lie, and that the reader has not been imposed upon. A description of invisibility is not a complaint about dishonesty.
distractors.seductive_element: The vocabulary of warrants and undertakings in the fourth paragraph is the vocabulary of honesty, and a reader who has been told that unreliability is invisible naturally reaches for the remedy.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the account the second paragraph grants to somebody else, and grants only as an account of what the device does for the writer. The passage's objection is not that it is false but that it answers a different question, so chiefly for is the word that cannot stand.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage endorses this account in unusually warm terms, calling it true and worth knowing, and a reader who registers the endorsement without the restriction will treat it as shared ground.

questions.target_mistake: taking an explanation of one effect for an explanation of the whole literary value of the technique
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to state the limit before the options: the account covers the sensation of access and stops short of why any particular writer's version succeeds.
questions.stem: The author's grammatical account is presented as reaching

options.A: the sensation of access and no further, since it cannot say why one writer's version convinces where another's does not
options.B: every mode in which a novel represents a character's thinking, since the reported and the quoted forms raise the same question
options.C: the question of when and why the technique spread through the fiction of nineteenth-century Europe
options.D: the charge that readers of such passages are deceived about what they have been told

explanation.expert_notice: The last paragraph draws the line itself and in two stages. The word illusion is restricted to an optician's sense, and then the account is confined: it explains the sensation and not the achievement, since why one writer's pages read like a mind is a question about the ear that the grammar does not answer.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that confinement. The explanation is a claim about what produces a particular experience, and the passage's closing sentence measures what has been won, calling it a smaller thing, namely why the good ones are able to work at all. An option that widens the account beyond the experience has taken the explanation past the sentence in which the author stopped it.
explanation.question_type_note: A scope question is usually answered in the paragraph where the author draws his own line rather than in the one where he makes his case. Look for the sentence that says what the argument does not cover.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author says what his account explains and not, write both halves down. Wrong options in scope questions substitute a limit the passage happens to mention for the limit the passage actually sets.

distractors.why_wrong: The explanation is the absence of a verb the other two forms contain, so it cannot cover them. The passage uses them throughout as the contrast that makes the third form's effect visible, and attributes the effect to only one of the three.
distractors.seductive_element: All three sentences are given in the first paragraph and discussed together, which makes the passage look like a general treatment of how novels render thought.

distractors.why_wrong: No history appears anywhere. The passage works entirely with three constructed sentences and with what readers report, and its only claim about origins is a refusal to make one, since it explains a consequence of the form rather than anybody's adoption of it.
distractors.seductive_element: A technique with a name and a tradition invites a historical treatment, and readers supply the chronology such essays usually contain.

distractors.why_wrong: The sixth paragraph refuses this charge rather than reaching it, saying no claim is made, nothing in the sentence could be a lie, and the reader has not been imposed upon. The account is expressly kept away from the moral sense of illusion.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the fourth paragraph really does say the reader has least to go on where the sensation is strongest, and deception is the conclusion that pairing invites.

questions.target_mistake: accepting a purpose for the technique that the passage never states, because purposes are what discussions of technique usually supply
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true, according to the passage?

options.A: A reported thought contains a verb that names somebody as doing the reporting
options.B: The third form keeps the narrator's tense and person while using the character's words
options.C: The sense of access weakens where the wording might have come from either party
options.D: The technique was developed in order to keep the narrator's judgements out of sight

explanation.expert_notice: Three of the four statements sit in named places: the verb of reporting and the agent it names in the third paragraph, the tense and person in the same paragraph, the failure under neutral diction in the fifth. No paragraph says why anybody began using the device.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The statement that is not true of the passage is the one about development and concealment. The only purpose the passage discusses belongs to the account it concedes, where the novelist remains present in the sentence and colours a thought without interrupting it, which is the opposite of keeping judgements out of sight. Everything the passage says about the form's effects is offered as a consequence of its grammar rather than as anybody's design.
explanation.question_type_note: In a NOT-true question three options restate the passage and one adds something. The addition is very often a purpose, since readers expect an explanation of a practice to say why it was adopted.
explanation.reading_habit: Separate what a passage says a form does from what it says anybody intended. Explanations by mechanism contain no intentions, and options that supply one are the standard way of testing whether you noticed.

distractors.why_wrong: The third paragraph states this as the first step of its argument: a verb of reporting names an agent, and an agent implies a channel. The option is that sentence with the technical word replaced.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage puts it in the vocabulary of agents and channels, so a reader hunting for the word reporter finds nothing and doubts the match.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the third paragraph's description of what the deletion leaves behind: the character's words, her rhythm, her exasperation, all of it inside the narrator's tense and person.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage gives the point through a list of particulars while the option states it as a general rule, which makes a faithful summary look like an addition.

distractors.why_wrong: The fifth paragraph states this as the prediction that earns the account its keep, reporting that neutral passages are read as commentary however faithfully they keep the form.
distractors.seductive_element: It reads as a qualification rather than as a claim, and readers hunting for the false statement discount anything that sounds like a hedge.

questions.target_mistake: supporting the view that the device adds depth, which is the account the passage replaces, instead of the view that the effect comes from a deletion
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the strengthener will isolate the deleted verb as the variable, holding everything else in the sentence constant.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's explanation of the effect?

options.A: Readers given the same sentence with and without its reporting verb describe the version without it as the less mediated
options.B: Novelists most often praised for psychological depth use this form more than other novelists do
options.C: Passages written in this form run on average rather longer than passages of quoted thought
options.D: The form has its strongest effect in novels whose narrators comment openly on their characters

explanation.expert_notice: The explanation is a claim about one variable. Everything is held constant, the words, the rhythm, the tense and person, and only the verb of reporting is removed, which the third paragraph states in exactly those terms before concluding that the access is manufactured by a subtraction.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that claim under test. Holding a sentence fixed and varying only the verb isolates the thing the passage says is doing the work, and a difference in how mediated the two versions feel is the effect the account predicts. Nothing else about either sentence can explain the difference, which is what makes this support rather than mere consistency.
explanation.question_type_note: A strengthen question asks what would prop the step from evidence to conclusion. Where an explanation names one variable, the strongest support is whatever varies that one thing and nothing else.
explanation.reading_habit: Name the author's causal claim in the form only X changed before reading the options. The strengthener is the one that changes only X, and the commonest distractor supports the explanation the author rejected.

distractors.why_wrong: An association between the form and a reputation for depth leaves the mechanism untouched, and it fits the account the passage denies, in which something is added to the characterisation. The passage insists that nothing whatever has been added.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because depth is what the effect feels like from inside, and evidence about novelists who are admired for it looks like evidence about the effect.

distractors.why_wrong: Length is never part of the account. The explanation concerns what a single sentence does and does not contain, and a difference in the average length of passages bears on neither the deleted verb nor the idiom.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like a measured, empirical finding about the very forms the passage contrasts, and empirical findings feel like support whatever they measure.

distractors.why_wrong: Open commentary restores the thing the explanation says must be missing, a visible narrator with a channel of his own, so this would tell against the account rather than for it.
distractors.seductive_element: The second paragraph does insist the novelist remains present in the sentence, and a reader who keeps that concession will take a visible narrator for a friendly fact.

vocabulary.passage_use: carries the character's idiom inside the narrator's grammar
vocabulary.meaning_here: the particular manner of speaking that marks one person out

vocabulary.passage_use: nowhere for the reader to locate the mediation
vocabulary.meaning_here: the passing of something through an intervening party

vocabulary.passage_use: A verb of reporting is also a warrant
vocabulary.meaning_here: an undertaking by which somebody stands behind a statement

vocabulary.passage_use: Passages in which the diction is neutral
vocabulary.meaning_here: the choice of words considered as a mark of who is speaking

mentor.challenge: A famous explanation of this technique is stated generously and then declared an answer to a different question. Keep track of which question each paragraph is answering, because four of the six questions turn on that.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: The sensation of being inside a character's mind is produced not by the doubling of voices that the usual account describes but by the deletion of the reporting verb, which leaves no agent and therefore no place for the reader to locate any mediation, and the same deletion removes the undertaking that makes an unreliable report detectable, so the mode that feels most knowing is the one that offers least to go on, though the illusion is optical rather than dishonest and the account explains the effect without explaining why any particular novelist brings it off.
mentor.main_idea: Readers report being inside a character's thinking, and only one of the three ways of rendering a thought produces it. The usual explanation, that two voices share the sentence, describes what the device does for the writer. What it does to the reader is explained by a subtraction: the verb of reporting is gone, so no agent is named, so there is nowhere to put the distance. The same subtraction removes the warrant that makes unreliability detectable. The account predicts that the effect fails when the wording is nobody's in particular, which it does, and it stops short of saying why any given writer succeeds.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Ask people what a novel was about and they summarise it. Ask what reading it was like and, with certain novels, they say something odd: not that they were told what a character was thinking, but that they were inside the thinking as it happened.

Take one moment written three ways. First: I shall have to answer it tonight, she thought. Second: She thought that she would have to answer it that night. Third: The letter would have to be answered tonight; there was no getting round it. Only the third gives you that feeling.

The usual explanation is that the third sentence has two people in it at once. It uses her words but the narrator's grammar, so the author can stay in the room while appearing to have left, and can tint a thought without breaking into it. The author of this passage says that is true and useful, and that it explains what the writer gets. It does not explain what the reader feels, because what the reader feels is that nobody is there at all.

His explanation is about grammar, and it is about something missing. The first two sentences both contain a verb of reporting, she thought. A verb like that names somebody doing the reporting, and once you have a reporter you have a route the thought travelled along, and the reader puts a little distance along that route. The third sentence has thrown that verb away and kept everything else: her words, her rhythm, her irritation, sitting inside the narrator's tense. Now nothing in the sentence names anyone passing the thought on. There is no place to put the distance, so the thought feels as if it arrived directly. The closeness comes from taking something out. Nothing extra was put in.

Then the uncomfortable part. That little verb was also a promise. If a narrator tells you she thought something, the narrator has vouched for it, and a promise can be broken, which is how you catch an unreliable narrator out: there is a statement on the page you can refuse to believe. The third sentence makes no statement and gives you nobody who could be wrong. So the way of writing that makes you feel you know a mind best is the one where you have the least to go on, and its unreliability does not look like a mistake. It just cannot be seen.

How do we know this explanation is right? Because it predicts where the trick stops working. If the feeling depends on the words being unmistakably hers, it should fade when the sentence could have come from either of them. And it does: write it in flat, anonymous language and readers experience commentary, however correctly the form is kept. The rival explanation predicts nothing here, since two voices are in the flat sentence just as much as in the vivid one.

Finally, two limits. Illusion here means what it means to an optician: a reliable appearance with a known cause, not a trick. Nothing is claimed in such a sentence, so nothing in it can be a lie, and you have not been taken in. And the account explains the feeling, not the art. Why one novelist's pages sound like a mind and another's like an impersonation is a question about the ear, and grammar has nothing to say about it. What grammar explains is why the good ones can work at all.
mentor.why_difficult: The rival explanation is conceded warmly and never called false, so it stays available as an answer for the whole passage, and readers who take the concession for agreement will assign the author a position he has expressly declined. The second difficulty is the fourth paragraph, where the same fact that produces the passage's most attractive claim produces its most uncomfortable one: the deletion gives the reader the strongest sense of knowing and the least to go on, and readers habitually keep only one of the two. The third is the last paragraph, which restricts the word illusion and confines the account, and both restrictions arrive after most readers have finished forming their view.
mentor.author_intention: To move the explanation of a familiar literary effect off the author and on to the sentence, and then to stop the reader turning the result into either a compliment about depth or a charge of deception.

paragraph_journey.note: Readers of some novels say they were inside the thinking. One moment written three ways, and only the third produces it.
The familiar explanation is about two voices sharing the sentence. True, and about what the writer gains, not about what the reader feels.
The reporting verb is gone. No verb, no agent; no agent, no channel; no channel, nowhere to put the distance. The closeness comes from a deletion.
That verb was also a promise somebody could break. Without it there is nothing to disbelieve, so unreliability in this mode is not caught, it is invisible.
It predicts the effect should fail when the words are nobody's in particular, and it does. The rival account predicts nothing here.
Illusion in the optician's sense, not deception. And the account explains the feeling, never why one writer brings it off and another does not.

mentor.tone_progression: It opens conversationally, almost as a report of what readers say; becomes generous while the rival explanation is set out; turns technical and exact through the grammatical argument; darkens briefly at the invisible unreliability; and closes carefully, defining a word and shrinking a claim rather than enlarging it.
key_transitions: 'It does not explain what the sentence does to the reader.' (paragraph 2): the concession is made and its boundary is drawn in one sentence.
'The access is manufactured by a subtraction.' (paragraph 3): the explanation arrives, and the following sentence denies that anything was added.
'Two limits should be entered here, and the first is a limit on the word illusion.' (opening of paragraph 6): the author refuses two conclusions his own argument invites.
mentor.misunderstanding: Two wrong models form. The first has the passage saying that this technique reveals more of a character than the alternatives, which reverses the mechanism, since the explanation is a deletion and the fourth paragraph says the reader has least to go on. The second has the passage exposing a deception, built out of the invisible unreliability and finished before the final paragraph arrives to restrict the word illusion to its optical sense. Both survive because the corrective sentences are short, flat, and late.
mentor.traps_summary: The set offers the conceded explanation as the author's, the acknowledged limit as the title, added depth in place of a subtraction, the moral sense of illusion in place of the optical one, a purpose the passage never assigns, and support for the rejected account in place of support for the accepted one. Asking which paragraph an option belongs to, and whether the author was still holding it at the end, answers all six.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an author concedes a rival explanation instead of refuting it, find the sentence that says what question the concession answers. Passages built this way keep the conceded view alive for every question that follows, and the commonest error is to hand the author a position he has politely accepted from somebody else. The second habit this passage rewards is to watch what else disappears when something is removed: an explanation by subtraction almost always has a second consequence, and that is where the hardest inference will be.
mentor.real_world: The same structure appears wherever confidence is produced by the removal of a visible intermediary: a summary with no named source, a recommendation with no disclosed sponsor, a translated remark with no translator credited, an automated decision with no officer to ask. In each the sense of directness rises exactly as the party who could be wrong disappears.
mentor.takeaway: The sentence that makes you feel closest to another mind is the one with nobody left in it to be mistaken.
mentor.reflection_question: Which of the things you feel you know directly reached you through somebody whose name was never in the sentence?
